summary: The note explores how rituals and superstitions persist in modern daily life, from morning routines and technology to sports, weddings, and death customs. It draws on interviews conducted in late 2023 with an anthropologist, a historian, and people from various professions. Its main argument is that superstitions arise from a human need for control and predictability, and that they evolve rather than fade.
one_line: An exploration of how superstitions and rituals persist across daily life, work, relationships, and death, based on 2023 interviews about their psychological and historical roots.
key_facts: Superstitions are described as born from the human desire for control and predictability in an unpredictable world.
On October 6, 2023, Dr. Emily Thompson, a cultural anthropologist at the University of Tradition and Mythology, said superstitions act as "a psychological safety net."
Susan Hill from Minnesota always exits her home with her right foot first, a practice taught by her mother to ensure a good day.
The aversion to the number 13, including omitting it from floor numbering in buildings, is particularly visible when the 13th falls on a Friday, a Western cultural imprint.
On September 20, 2023, Spanish teacher Carlos Garcia said people in his culture touch wood or iron when talking about future hopes to avoid tempting fate.
On September 29, 2023, restaurant owner Sarah Zhang described hanging charms over doorways to attract luck and customers, and placing mirrors to deflect negative energy.
On November 3, 2023, Silicon Valley programmer Tim Jackson admitted he crosses his fingers before deploying new software despite his logic-based work.
Actors avoid saying "Macbeth" in a theater and call it "The Scottish Play" to stave off bad luck.
Wedding superstitions include the groom not seeing the bride before the wedding and not giving knives as gifts, lest they sever relationships.
On October 21, 2023, wedding planner Maryam Naseer said couples want the dress color and ceremony date to align with practices they believe bring lifelong happiness.
On November 15, 2023, Marcus Chan, a funeral director in New Orleans, explained that diverse communities have unique practices to ensure the soul's peaceful passing.

On December 1, 2023, French historian Marie Dupont explained that throwing spilled salt over the shoulder began because salt was precious and spilling it was thought to draw the ire of spirits or the devil.
